challenges.name: allowlist-quarantine-quiz
challenges.title: Who approved this name, and how old is this version?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the CodeDev dependency gate: an allowlist matcher with a wildcard entry, and an exception for an urgent security release.

questions.question:
The gate's allowlist matcher, written by an AI assistant:

const allowlist = ["@codedev/*", "lodash*", "zod"];
const allowed = (name: string) =>
  allowlist.some((p) => p.endsWith("*") ? name.startsWith(p.slice(0, -1)) : name === p);

Policy: quarantineDays 7. Today is 2026-10-27.
Pull request #2331 adds lodash-deep-clone-pro 1.0.3, published 2026-10-18T09:00:00Z by an account created the same day.

Statement: "The gate blocks lodash-deep-clone-pro in pull request #2331."
questions.explanation: False. For "lodash*" the matcher drops the star and checks name.startsWith("lodash"), which lodash-deep-clone-pro passes. The version is 9 days old, so the 7-day quarantine ends on 2026-10-25 and does not block it either: the package is allowed. A wildcard is safe only for a scope you own, because only your organization can publish under @codedev/; anyone can register a name that starts with lodash. The misconception is that a prefix pattern restricts names the way a scope does; replace it with the exact names you approved (lodash, lodash.merge ...).

True. 4.22.1 is one day old, so the quarantine alone would block it until 2026-11-02, but the exception matches the name and the exact version and is valid until 2026-11-03, so the gate allows it. The exception says nothing about 4.22.2: a release tomorrow is checked like any other version and waits 7 days. That is the reason exceptions name an exact version - an exception for "express" in general would also have let through a hijacked release published right after the fix. The misconception is that an exception approves a package; it approves one decision about one version, for a limited time.

challenges.name: dependency-allowlist-gate
challenges.title: Gate new dependencies: allowlist, quarantine and exceptions
challenges.description:
Every pull request to the CodeDev repositories passes a dependency gate before npm ci. Write decide(change, policy, registry, today) in TypeScript: it returns { allow, reasons } for one added or updated package (change.name and the new version change.to; from is only displayed). Blocking reasons, in this order: "not in registry" - registry (name -> version -> publish timestamp) has no such package or no such version; "publish date unknown" - the timestamp is not ISO 8601 with a date, a time (hh:mm, optional :ss and fraction) and Z or an offset such as +07:00 (2026-10-20T08:15:00Z, 2026-10-21T03:00:00+07:00); "not on allowlist" - no allowlist entry matches: an entry matches the exact name (case-sensitive), and an entry of the form "@scope/*" matches every name that starts with "@scope/"; "quarantined until (published

)" - P is the UTC calendar date (YYYY-MM-DD) of the publish instant, D is P plus policy.quarantineDays days, and the version is blocked while today < D (today is a YYYY-MM-DD date; dates in this form compare correctly as strings). An exception { name, version, ticket, expires } matches a change with the same name and exact version; it is valid while expires is a real calendar date written YYYY-MM-DD and today <= expires. A valid exception lifts "not on allowlist" and the quarantine, but never "not in registry" or "publish date unknown"; when it turns a block into an allow, reasons is ["exception (expires )"] for the first valid matching exception in the list. When the change stays blocked and matching exceptions exist but none of them is valid, add "exception not valid (expires )" for the first matching one, as the last reason. A change with no blocking reason is allowed with reasons []. The runner prints one line per change, in input order, then the totals.
hints: Which blocking reasons describe facts about the package (does this version exist, can we read its date) and which describe your team's decisions (an approved name, a waiting period)? Which of the two kinds can a signed-off exception change?

Collect the reasons in two lists - the ones an exception may lift and the ones it may not - and look at exceptions only at the end. For dates: check the timestamp format with a regular expression before Date.parse (which accepts many other formats), take new Date(ms).toISOString().slice(0, 10) for the UTC date, add days in milliseconds from that date's midnight UTC, and compare YYYY-MM-DD strings. A real date survives the round trip through Date and toISOString unchanged.

A worked example on other data, quarantine 3 days, today 2026-03-10: a version published 2026-03-07T22:00:00-05:00 is 2026-03-08T03:00:00Z, so P = 2026-03-08 and D = 2026-03-11: blocked. One published 2026-03-07T10:00:00Z gives D = 2026-03-10: allowed, because today is not before D. An entry @acme/* allows @acme/cli but not @acme-tools/cli or acme-cli. An exception that expires 2026-03-10 still counts on 2026-03-10; one for version 2.0.0 does nothing for 2.0.1.
